title: 'Restless' and 'Harlem Butterfly' and the puzzling Mercer sheet music
summary: She learned 'Restless' at Le Ruban Bleu; the sheet music credits puzzle them, as does a cover with Julie London.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: But you recorded that in 1948 for the Apollo label.
Yes.
On that mysterious session that --

Right. Well, 'Restless' is a very old song. I had heard it long before I recorded it. And I don't think I ever heard Helen Ward's recording of it. And 'Closest Pages In A Book' -- that's another oldie -- I like to select material, although it's old, it fits in today. You may or may not call them standards, but I think they're good tunes, and they are a little unusual. They're not the usual AABA, as you would say. And they just happen to be songs that stuck in my memory. 'Harlem Butterfly', I had been doing as far back as 1941. I heard a guitar -- Johnny Johnson, a guitar play -- sing 'Harlem Butterfly' on an early

radio show, and I liked it.
And I never saw the music to it, but --
I was appearing at Le Ruban Bleu at the time, and I
sang it over, and we sort of worked out the changes
with Herman Chittison.
And I began doing 'Harlem Butterfly.' And
I later found out that it was a Johnny Mercer tune.
And one of the things that we're puzzled
about is the fact that the sheet music, number one,
it has 'words and music by Johnny Mercer,' and nobody
recalls that Johnny Mercer ever wrote any music or
songs -- he was a lyricist.
And number two, the cover on the sheet
music has -- I can't think of her name at the
present time.
(Pause)
The singer whose picture is on the
cover of the music is Julie London.
Mrs. Bobby Troup.
That's right.

But the strange thing about it, 'Harlem
Butterfly' is the song that would be more of a thing
that Billie Holiday would do rather than Julie London,

if you know what I mean.
Yes.
Well also, the chronology seems odd, because I think she made a name for herself in the 1950's.
Yeah.
And the song is much older than that.
That's right.
I don't know. As I said before, I hadn't seen the sheet music. And, of course, when I decided to record it, Bob got the sheet music on all these tunes.so that he would have something to go by.
And it just appears to me that they just went ahead and printed up some copies real fast and put Julie London's picture on there, because they didn't know what else to do.
You've never recorded that song before, have you?
No, I haven't recorded 'Harlem Butterfly' before. But it's a beautiful tune.
